cards.front: {{c1::Concentration}} is how much of a substance is in a given space.
cards.quote: Concentration is how much of a substance is in a given space.
cards.section: Explain: particles spread from more to less

cards.front: {{c1::Diffusion}} is the movement of a substance from where it is more concentrated to where it is less concentrated.
cards.quote: Diffusion is the movement of a substance from where it is more concentrated to where it is less concentrated.
cards.section: Explain: particles spread from more to less

cards.front: Why does a substance drift from a crowded side to a less crowded side, even though nothing pushes it?
cards.back: Particles are always moving at random. On average, more of them leave the crowded side than come back.
cards.quote: Particles are always moving at random, so on average more of them leave a crowded side than come back.

cards.front: Why are diffusion and osmosis called passive transport?
cards.back: The cell spends no energy moving the particles. They drift from more concentrated to less concentrated on their own.
cards.quote: A substance that can cross drifts from where it is more concentrated (more crowded) to where it is less concentrated, with no push from the cell.

cards.front: A drop of food colouring spreads through a glass of still water until the colour looks even. Are the dye particles still moving? Why does the colour stop changing?
cards.back: Yes, they keep moving. Once the dye is even, about as many particles move each way, so the overall drift ends.
cards.quote: In a glass, the drift ends once the dye is even.
cards.section: Explain: particles spread from more to less

cards.front: In a glass, diffusion of dye stops once it is even. Why does oxygen keep diffusing into your cells instead of stopping?
cards.back: Your cells keep using oxygen, so oxygen stays scarce inside and keeps diffusing in.
cards.quote: Your cells keep using oxygen, so oxygen stays scarce inside and keeps diffusing in.
cards.section: Explain: particles spread from more to less

cards.front: A busy cell keeps making carbon dioxide. Which way does carbon dioxide move across its membrane, and does the cell spend energy on it?
cards.back: Out of the cell, by diffusion, with no energy from the cell.
cards.why: Carbon dioxide is more concentrated inside, where it is made, so it drifts toward the outside where there is less.
cards.quote: They keep making carbon dioxide, so it keeps diffusing out (that lesson).
cards.section: Explain: particles spread from more to less

cards.front: The cell membrane is {{c1::selectively permeable}}: it lets some substances through and holds back others.
cards.quote: It is selectively permeable: it lets some substances through and holds back others.
cards.section: Explain: water crosses a choosy membrane

cards.front: In most cells, which three substances cross the cell membrane easily?
cards.back: Water, oxygen and carbon dioxide. Dissolved particles such as salt and sugar cross much less easily.
cards.quote: In most cells, water, oxygen and carbon dioxide cross it easily.
cards.section: Explain: water crosses a choosy membrane

cards.front: In osmosis, water moves from more water to less water, which is toward the side with {{c1::more dissolved particles}}.
cards.back: The cell spends no energy on it.
cards.quote: Key idea: In osmosis, water moves from more water to less water, which is toward the side with more dissolved particles, and the cell spends no energy on it.

cards.front: In the model, salt cannot cross a membrane but water can. Why does water drift toward the salty side?
cards.back: The dissolved salt leaves a little less water on its side. Water drifts from more water to less water, so it moves toward the salt.
cards.quote: Dissolved particles that cannot cross leave a little less water on their side, so water drifts toward the side with more of them.

cards.front: When osmosis seems to stop, have water molecules stopped crossing the membrane?
cards.back: No. Water keeps crossing both ways. The overall drift stops once as much water leaves as enters.
cards.quote: The overall drift stops once as much water leaves as enters.

cards.front: Salt is sprinkled on cucumber slices. Within about 15 minutes, drops of water bead up on top. Which way did water move, and why?
cards.back: Out of the cucumber cells, toward the salt outside.
cards.why: The membrane holds most of the salt back, so the outside has more dissolved particles. Water drifts toward that side, with no energy from the cells.
cards.quote: In salty water, like the cucumber, water leaves.

cards.front: Limp lettuce leaves sit in plain cold water and turn crisp. The inside of the leaf cells still has more dissolved particles than the water. Why does water stop coming in?
cards.back: The swelling cell presses on its stiff cell wall, and the wall presses back. That push stops the drift and keeps the leaf crisp.
cards.why: Water moves toward more dissolved particles, but a push back, such as from a cell wall, can stop the drift before the sides are even.
cards.quote: That push stops the drift and keeps the leaf crisp, even though the inside still has more dissolved particles.

cards.front: A red blood cell, an animal cell with no cell wall, is put in plain water. What could happen, and why?
cards.back: It can swell until it bursts.
cards.why: The cell has more dissolved particles than plain water, so water drifts in. With no wall to push back, nothing stops it.
cards.quote: With no wall to push back, water keeps coming in: a red blood cell in plain water can swell until it bursts.

cards.front: How does the cell membrane help with homeostasis?
cards.back: By letting some things pass and holding others back, it helps keep the right amounts of water and other substances inside the cell.
cards.quote: By letting some things pass and holding others back, it helps keep the right amounts of water and other substances inside the cell.

cards.front: A cucumber slice in salty water went from 26 g to 21 g overnight. What was its percent change in mass?
cards.back: (21 − 26) ÷ 26 × 100 = −5 ÷ 26 × 100, about −19 percent. The slice lost mass, so water left it.
cards.quote: percent change in mass = (final mass − starting mass) ÷ starting mass × 100
cards.section: Elaborate: weigh cucumber slices in salt and plain water

cards.front: In the cucumber demonstration, one slice started at 26 g and the other at 22 g. Why is percent change a fairer way to compare them than grams?
cards.back: The slices started at different masses. Percent change compares each change to that slice's own starting mass.
cards.quote: Why is percent change a fairer way to compare the two slices than grams?
cards.section: Elaborate: weigh cucumber slices in salt and plain water

cards.front: In the cucumber demonstration, masses were read only to the nearest gram. The slice in distilled water went from 22 g to 23 g in 1 hour (+5%). Why might this gain not be real?
cards.back: Rounding to the nearest gram could make each percent change off by a few percent, so this small gain could even be zero.
cards.why: The overnight changes are far larger than this rounding error, so those can be trusted more.
cards.quote: The smallest one, the 1-hour gain in distilled water, could even be zero.
cards.section: Elaborate: weigh cucumber slices in salt and plain water

cards.front: You test how the amount of salt in water changes the mass of potato pieces. Name the independent variable, the dependent variable and the control.
cards.back: Independent: grams of salt in each 100 mL of water. Dependent: percent change in mass of each piece. Control: the cup with 0 g of salt (plain water).
cards.quote: Control: the cup with 0 g of salt, which is plain water.

cards.front: In a class test, potato pieces gain mass in plain water and lose more mass as the salt goes up. Does this fit osmosis? Explain.
cards.back: Yes. In plain water, water moves into the cells; in salt water, it moves out toward the salt. More salt means more water leaves.
cards.why: Water drifts toward the side with more dissolved particles, with no energy from the cells.
cards.quote: If pieces gain mass in plain water and lose more as the salt goes up, that fits osmosis.
